this year we significantly transformed project workflows across all departments, enabling us to iterate much faster and take on projects with deadlines that previously seemed impossible.

The biggest challenge in branding projects is not making nice pictures, but getting the client to believe in those nice pictures. A big portion of the budget for large branding projects doesn't go into implementation, but into communication, presentations, and sometimes redundant iterations that show stakeholders what we considered, what didn't work, and why we ended up going in this direction.

If you send a batch of concepts without any reasoning, thinking someone will just get your vision or blindly trust your expertise, don't be surprised if your concepts get rejected.

65 prompts + a little bit of manual fine tuning in Blender.

With AI you have to approach tasks differently to be efficient and fast.

For @polyester , we're currently building an AI native system that would speed up video and 3D production while keeping things on-brand, and not just relying on one prompt to design everything.

Instead of simply doing a one-off 3D asset in Blender or a video in After Effects, you use a more systematic approach by creating a collection of reusable text transitions, timings, references, intro/outro variations, etc.

So later on, you can experiment much faster with AI, generating dozens of options overnight and then fine-tuning the ones that work.

Dear @claudeai, you have amazing models, and you probably have even better ones available internally. Could you please ask your Super Intelligence to simply copy the UX of the Codex desktop app? Their app is obviously better.

Your quality bar for UX/design is much lower than Codex’s or Cursor’s. It would be amazing to fix that.

So far, you have a competitive advantage in the design community: your models are simply better at motion and design, so I still have to use your app for certain tasks. But it’s extremely painful to use your application after experiencing better alternatives.

I did an interesting experiment today. I fed Opus 5.5 one of our Figma tutorials from two years ago and asked it to reimplement it in Blender. It worked remarkably well.

What surprised me most was how accurately it copied the timings. It took just three prompts to get to that point. Very impressive result.

I honestly don't understand many new design tools. There are Pencil, Paper, Elyx, MagicPath, and many more launching each month. Great designers are behind them, and it feels like many people use them. But I feel so disconnected from their approach to design.

Let me share my thoughts. 

They all have a middleman issue. What you design is not what you ship. We're in the age of AI. I want to see the exact behavior of my components, I want to see the exact "rendering"/"look" of my components. Why do I need a canvas that shows me just "designs"? We had that already in Figma for many years. Authors of those tools can argue with me, saying, "But we're much closer to the code than Figma. We use HTML/React or whatever to render your designs." Great, but it's not the same code anyway.

From that issue comes another one, a lack of a single source of truth. Design lives in two places again. Users see the one that is built in code, while designers look at their versions on the canvas.

Then you can tell me, "Come on, I'm a designer, not a developer. I need a canvas. Those apps give me a canvas." Do you know that you can ask AI to bring you a canvas into the actual project you're working on?

"But building code is slow, I need something simpler just to quickly iterate on my design ideas." Again, what's the problem with asking your Claude/Codex to solve that thing for you? AI can stop running tests/linters/performance checks, or simply make some drafts on that canvas for you in plain HTML/CSS, exactly like those tools do. But if you want to do something more complicated, nothing can stop you.

Which brings us to another point. Those are closed-source tools. I like to adapt my environment to my needs and my tasks. I don't want to wait anymore for companies to decide to prioritize or build something that's important to me, or support the AI client that someone uses (recent Figma drama). Software development has become cheap. Bringing any controls or canvases into your environment is not an issue if you need them.

I still use Figma, more like a sketchpad or for some brand work, but I don't understand why I would want to switch to something else if those tools fundamentally have the same problem as Figma.

For me, those tools still feel like they're made for designers who haven't figured out yet what AI is capable of. And I'm not talking about letting AI design instead of you. I'm talking about letting AI create the environment for you, which can be much more powerful and more efficient for the exact tasks that you or your team work on.
